title: Distributed Data Systems
summary: Replication, partitioning, consensus, and the consistency models that govern distributed data — plus the modern patterns (CRDTs, lakehouse, HTAP) shaping the next generation of systems.

chapters.title: Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems
chapters.summary: Three properties any data system must balance — reliability under faults, scalability under growth, maintainability under change — and the precise vocabulary for each (faults vs failures, percentiles, tail latency, operability, evolvability).

chapters.title: Data Models and Query Languages
chapters.summary: The major data-model families — relational, document, graph, with their query-language paradigms — the impedance mismatch problem, polyglot persistence, and how property graphs differ from triple-stores.

chapters.title: Storage and Retrieval
chapters.summary: How storage engines actually work under the hood — log-structured (LSM-trees, SSTables, Bloom filters) vs page-oriented (B-trees, WAL), plus the analytics-storage detour into column stores, star schemas, and data warehouses.

chapters.title: Encoding and Evolution
chapters.summary: Wire formats (JSON, Protobuf, Avro, Thrift) and the patterns for evolving data without downtime — schema registries, field-tag compatibility rules, and how data flows through databases, services, and async messaging.

chapters.title: Replication
chapters.summary: Keeping data on multiple machines — three strategies (single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless), their consistency consequences (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), and the quorum / sloppy-quorum / hinted-handoff vocabulary.

chapters.title: Partitioning
chapters.summary: Splitting data across nodes — by key range, by hash of key, with hot-spot awareness — plus the operational shape of secondary indexes (local vs global), rebalancing strategies, consistent hashing, and request routing.

chapters.title: Transactions
chapters.summary: ACID vs BASE, the weak isolation levels real databases give you (read committed, snapshot isolation, MVCC), the bugs each level lets through (dirty reads, lost updates, write skew, phantom reads), and the three roads to true serialisability (actual serial execution, 2PL, SSI).

chapters.title: The Trouble with Distributed Systems
chapters.summary: Networks, clocks, and processes are all unreliable — the vocabulary for partial failure: unreliable networks, congestion, monotonic vs time-of-day clocks, clock drift, stop-the-world pauses, fencing tokens, split brain, and Byzantine faults.

chapters.title: Consistency and Consensus
chapters.summary: The densest chapter in the book — linearizability vs serialisability, ordering guarantees (causal, total, FIFO), Lamport timestamps, CAP / PACELC, two- and three-phase commit, consensus and FLP impossibility, and Paxos / Raft with epoch numbers and fencing.

chapters.title: Batch Processing
chapters.summary: The Hadoop → Spark / Flink lineage for bounded data sets — MapReduce, the shuffle phase, sort-merge / broadcast / partitioned hash joins, dataflow engines, DAGs of operators, fault tolerance via re-computation, and bulk synchronous parallel.

chapters.title: Stream Processing
chapters.summary: Processing unbounded data — log-based message brokers (Kafka model), partitioned logs, consumer groups, change data capture, event sourcing, the processing-time vs event-time distinction, watermarks, windowing patterns, and exactly-once semantics.

chapters.title: The Future of Data Systems
chapters.summary: Where Kleppmann's book points — data integration as the real problem, stream-table duality, the unbundled database, logs as a primary abstraction, CQRS, lambda vs kappa, the end-to-end argument, and correctness beyond schemas.

chapters.title: Modern Distributed Data Patterns
chapters.summary: What's emerged since 2017 — CRDTs in production (operation-based vs state-based), HTAP databases, the lakehouse architecture (Iceberg / Delta / Hudi), data mesh, vector indexes (pgvector / ANN), serverless OLTP, embedded analytics (DuckDB pattern), feature stores, time-series databases, and zero-ETL change feeds.
